slots.practicalActivity: Write one paragraph describing, for your own organization (or a past employer), one specific instance where two people or teams disagreed about what a number meant -- a metric, a customer count, a status field -- and don't solve it, just describe exactly what disagreed and why. Then write one sentence arguing why that data should be treated as a business asset, the way the company already treats cash or inventory.
slots.deliverable: A short written vignette naming a real definitional disagreement, plus one sentence framing the underlying data as a business asset.

lessons.title: Data Governance vs. Data Management vs. Data Quality

slots.practicalActivity: Take the vignette from the previous slot and sort it: is it a governance problem (no agreed decision rights), a management problem (the pipeline that moves the data), or a quality problem (the data itself is wrong)? Then estimate, in hours or dollars, what that specific disagreement actually cost the organization.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph classification of your vignette as governance, management, or quality (with reasoning), plus a rough cost estimate for the incident.

lessons.title: Governance Drivers: Compliance, Trust and Value

slots.practicalActivity: For your own organization, name which of the three drivers (compliance, trust, value) is the strongest argument for governance right now and why; then pick one common governance failure pattern from the lesson and write one sentence on a visible symptom of it you've actually seen.
slots.deliverable: A short written note naming the dominant driver with a one-sentence justification, plus one real or representative governance-failure symptom.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick any three of the ten DAMA-DMBOK knowledge areas surrounding governance on the DAMA Wheel and write one sentence per area giving a specific, real or researched example of that discipline in practice; then note which named framework (DMBOK, DCAM, COBIT, ISO/IEC 38505) seems best suited to your own organization's size and maturity, and why.
slots.deliverable: Three one-sentence DAMA knowledge-area examples, plus a short framework recommendation with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: Rate your own organization (or one you know) against a simple maturity scale (ad hoc, reactive, defined, managed, optimized), with one sentence of evidence for the rating; then describe in one paragraph which operating model shape (centralized, decentralized, federated, or a mix) seems to actually be running today, independent of what any org chart claims.
slots.deliverable: A maturity rating with supporting evidence, plus a short written assessment of the organization's actual (not official) operating model.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's 'signals' test (does a single body resolve cross-team data disagreements, or does the disagreement just persist?), confirm or revise your previous slot's operating-model assessment; then write a short recommendation for which model your organization should move toward, naming one concrete tradeoff you're accepting.
slots.deliverable: A short written operating-model recommendation naming the chosen model and one explicit tradeoff being accepted.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one data domain (customer, product, employee, or similar) from your own organization or a hypothetical one. Write one paragraph naming who currently makes the real business calls about that domain even informally, whether that person is currently treated as the owner, and who would be a natural data steward handling the day-to-day work.
slots.deliverable: A short written note naming a real or hypothetical data owner and steward for one domain, with reasoning for each choice.

slots.practicalActivity: For the same domain, name who would act as data custodian (the technical team actually storing/securing the data) and who the primary data consumers are; then sketch a lightweight governance council for your organization -- 4-6 named roles -- and one decision type that council alone would be authorized to make.
slots.deliverable: A short written note naming a custodian and consumers for your domain, plus a sketched council roster with one decision type scoped to it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a small RACI matrix with at least three real governance activities (e.g., approve a new business glossary term, approve a new quality rule, resolve a cross-team definition dispute) against the owner, steward, custodian, and consumer roles from this chapter. Check every row for exactly one A. Then name who in your organization would realistically serve as executive sponsor, and one piece of evidence they'd actually back the program.
slots.deliverable: A RACI matrix (at least 3 activities x 4 roles) with exactly one A per row, plus a named executive-sponsor candidate with supporting evidence.

slots.practicalActivity: Governance structure lab: without looking back at the lessons, draft a one-page governance org chart for a mid-size organization of your choosing -- name the operating model (centralized/decentralized/federated), one governance council with its members, a data owner and steward for two different domains, and a RACI matrix covering at least four activities across all four role types from this chapter.
slots.deliverable: A one-page governance org chart document: operating model, one council roster, owner/steward pairs for two domains, and a RACI matrix for four activities.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one real data policy statement (2-3 sentences) for a domain in your own organization: state the rule, state the reasoning, stay implementation-agnostic, and name who it applies to. Then write one companion standard that implements it with concrete detail (e.g., a specific field format, retention period, or encryption requirement).
slots.deliverable: One written policy statement paired with one implementing standard for the same domain.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a formal data definition and naming standard for one commonly ambiguous term in your organization (e.g., "active customer" or "completed order"), precise enough that two teams couldn't disagree about it; then sketch the policy lifecycle stages (draft, review, approve, publish, periodic review, retire) this definition would need to go through before it's official.
slots.deliverable: One precise written data definition with naming standard, plus a sketched policy-lifecycle stage list for getting it approved.

slots.practicalActivity: Name one concrete enforcement mechanism (automated check, access control, review gate) that would make the policy from two slots ago actually binding rather than a suggestion; then identify which regulation (GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, HIPAA, or a sector-specific rule) most applies to your organization's data and name one specific obligation it imposes.
slots.deliverable: A written enforcement mechanism for your earlier policy, plus one named regulation and one specific obligation it creates for your organization.

slots.practicalActivity: Run a quick readiness assessment on your own organization (rate pain, sponsorship, existing policy, and tooling as High/Medium/Low, with one sentence of evidence each). Then draft a one-page business case with four short sections: the problem in business terms, the proposed scope (one pilot-sized ask), required resources, and how you'd measure anticipated value.
slots.deliverable: A readiness rating across four dimensions with evidence, plus a one-page four-section business case.

slots.practicalActivity: Scope a 90-day governance pilot for the domain used in your business case: name the pilot domain, a baseline metric, and the pilot owner. Then sketch a six-month roadmap showing where this pilot sits (e.g., days 1-60 discovery/foundation, days 61-90 the pilot itself, months 3-6 expansion to a second domain if it succeeds).
slots.deliverable: A scoped 90-day pilot (domain, baseline metric, owner) plus a six-month roadmap sketch placing the pilot in sequence.

slots.practicalActivity: Draft a short announcement note (3-5 sentences) introducing your pilot to the teams affected, framed as an enabler rather than a new rule to follow. Then, following the lesson's Meridian Fulfillment Co. pattern, invent your own clearly fictional company and write a one-page synthesis walking a single data problem through all five chapters: the problem and its cost, the operating model that fits, the named owner/steward/sponsor with one RACI line, one policy and standard, and the readiness-to-pilot-to-roadmap-to-communication sequence.
slots.deliverable: A short pilot-announcement note, plus a one-page fictional-company synthesis covering all five chapters in sequence.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: write a two-page data governance charter for a real or realistic organization of your choosing, bringing together everything from this course -- the governance driver that matters most, the chosen operating model, a named owner/steward/council/sponsor structure with a RACI matrix, one policy with its companion standard, and a scoped 90-day pilot with a baseline metric and success criteria.
slots.deliverable: A two-page written data governance charter covering driver, operating model, roles/RACI, one policy+standard pair, and a scoped pilot with success criteria.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can assess an organization's governance maturity, choose and justify an operating model, assign and defend owner/steward/custodian roles with a working RACI matrix, write a real policy-and-standard pair, and scope a fundable 90-day governance pilot -- the structural vocabulary and playbook the rest of the Data Governance Engineer path assumes a student already has.
